paragraphs: Parents all over the world have the same complaint: their teenagers stay up late at night and are impossible to wake up in the morning. Many adults think this is simply laziness. Scientists, however, say the explanation is biological.

Our bodies have an internal clock that tells us when to feel sleepy and when to feel awake. During adolescence, this clock moves later. The brain starts producing melatonin, the hormone that makes us sleepy, about two hours later than it did in childhood. As a result, many teenagers do not feel tired until eleven o'clock or midnight, even if they are exhausted.

At the same time, sleep experts recommend that teenagers sleep between eight and ten hours a night. If school starts at eight o'clock and a student falls asleep at midnight, it is easy to see the problem. Lack of sleep has been linked to poor concentration, bad moods, weaker memory and more car accidents among young drivers.

Some schools have decided to start later. In several places in the United States and Europe where classes begin at half past eight or nine, researchers have found that students sleep more, arrive late less often and pay more attention in class. Not everyone agrees, though: later start times can be difficult for parents who work early and for schools that share buses.

Phones make things worse. The blue light from screens can delay sleep even more, and messages and videos keep the brain busy. Experts suggest switching off devices an hour before bed, keeping the same timetable at weekends and getting some sunlight in the morning.
So, next time a teenager refuses to get out of bed, remember: it may not be laziness at all.
